text: Hi, how's it going? I'm a big coffee lover, so I guess I'll start there. I can't really start my day without a cup of coffee, and this morning was no different. I had one before I came to take this test, and I'm already looking forward to another one once it's over. I work in IT, and my days are pretty busy. I live in an apartment, and I'm pretty much a homebody. In my free time, I like listening to music, playing computer games, and reading. So, yeah, that's me in a nutshell: coffee, music, and my computer. I'm happy to be here, and I hope I do well today!

Well, banks in Korea are everywhere. You can find one on almost every busy street, especially downtown and near big office buildings. They're usually in tall buildings, on the first or second floor, and often a few banks are right next to each other. Inside, they're clean and quiet. You take a number, and wait for your turn on a comfy sofa. And the staff are super polite. They bow and say, "How can I help you?" Also, there are ATMs at almost every convenience store, so you can get cash at midnight. And these days, we have mobile-only banks too, like KakaoBank. To sum up, banks here are convenient, friendly, and easy to find.

To be honest, I hardly ever go to the bank these days. I do most things on my banking app, like sending money and paying bills. But there are a few things I still have to do in person. For example, when I got a loan for my apartment, I had to sign a lot of papers. That took a whole afternoon! And before my trips abroad, I go to exchange money. The last time was before I went to Guam. I took a number, waited for twenty minutes, and got a pile of dollars. The teller was really nice, and she gave me a free coffee coupon. Of course, I loved that! So I only go when I really have to, but it's always a quick and easy visit.

Banks have changed a lot. When I was a kid, everything was on paper. I remember my dad taking me to the bank to open my first account. They gave me a little passbook, and the teller stamped it every time I put in money. I felt so important! Every time I saved my allowance, I'd go to check the number. And when I saw the interest, I felt like I was getting rich! Also, banks closed at 4 p.m., so you had to run there after school or work. The lines were really long, too. Now, it's totally different. I can do everything on my phone, 24 hours a day. I don't even need a card. It's so convenient, but part of me misses that little passbook.

Koreans love places where they can do something together. For example, a lot of people go hiking. On weekends, every mountain is full of people in colorful hiking gear! Another popular spot is a cafe. Honestly, we have a cafe on every corner, and people sit for hours, chatting or studying. Then there are noraebang, which are karaoke rooms, where friends sing their hearts out. And my personal favorite: the jjimjilbang. It's a Korean spa, with hot rooms and saunas. People relax, eat boiled eggs and sweet rice drink, and sleep on the floor. Young people also go to PC bangs to play games. I'd say Koreans are very social, so they like places where they can hang out with others.

When I was in college, my free time was all about games. My friends and I spent hours at the PC bang. We played StarCraft all night, and we'd walk out at sunrise feeling like zombies. I also played soccer on weekends. Back then, I had a lot of energy, and I never wanted to go home early. But things changed after I started working full time. Now I'm pretty much a homebody. I spend my free time reading, listening to music, or playing games at home. And I love sitting in a cafe with a good cup of coffee. So I went from the PC bang to the coffee shop! I still love games, but I need a lot more sleep these days. I guess I just got older.

The last time I had some real free time was last Saturday. I didn't have any work, so I said to my friend, "Let's go somewhere nice." We heard about a new cafe on the east side of my city, right on the beach. So we packed up and drove there. It was a beautiful day, and the ocean looked amazing. I ordered my usual americano, and my friend got a latte. We also shared a huge strawberry smoothie. We sat on the terrace for about two hours, just watching the waves. I brought my book, but I didn't even open it. My friend, on the other hand, was on his phone the whole time! Anyway, it was a simple day, but it was exactly what I needed.

My favorite place in Korea is Gangneung. As a coffee lover, it's like paradise to me. It's known as "the coffee city", and there's a famous coffee street right by the beach. You can get hand-drip coffee from a small cafe and drink it while looking at the ocean. It doesn't get much better than that! I've tried about ten cafes there already, and every one was different. Besides coffee, the beach is beautiful, and the seafood is really fresh. My friend loves the sunrise at the beach. Another place I enjoy is Gyeongju, because it's full of history, and it's so peaceful. But if I could pick only one, it would be Gangneung, no doubt.

When I was about ten, my family went to Seoraksan. My dad rented a big van, and all of us squeezed in. It was a total circus. Everybody sang loudly the whole way, and they fought over the seats by the window. Since I was the smallest, I always ended up in the middle. I got terribly carsick on those winding mountain roads, and my mom had to stop the van twice. Everybody laughed at me, of course. But once we got there, I forgot about it. We hiked a little, saw the huge waterfall, and ate picnic lunches on a big rock. My dad took a family photo, and we all look so happy. I still have that photo on my shelf.

I'll never forget what happened at Seoraksan a few years ago. My friend and I took the cable car up the mountain to see the fall leaves. The view was beautiful at first. But halfway up, the cable car suddenly stopped! It was swinging in the wind, and we were hanging in the air. The thing is, my friend is terrified of heights. She grabbed my arm, and her face went pale. I tried to stay calm, and I kept telling jokes. I said, "Look at the bright side. Great view, right?" She gave me a look. We were stuck there for about thirty minutes. Finally, the cable car started moving again, and we both let out a big sigh. When we got off, her legs were shaking, so we sat down for a cup of hot coffee. It was scary, but we laughed about it later. To this day, she says "no more cable cars!"

Hey, it's me. Thanks so much for inviting me to your holiday party! I can't wait. I have a few questions. First, what day is the party, and what time does it start?. Okay, got it. Should I bring anything? Maybe some food or drinks?. Sure, I'll bring a cake. Also, is there a dress code, or can I just wear something casual?. Great. And who else is coming? Will I know anyone?. One last thing: is there parking near your house, or should I take a taxi?. Perfect. Thanks again. See you at the party! And of course, I'll bring some coffee for the morning after!

Hey, it's me. I'm so sorry, but I have some bad news. I just had a car accident on my way to your house. Don't worry, I'm totally fine, and nobody was hurt. It was just a fender bender, but I have to wait for the police and my insurance company. So I'm going to be late. I feel terrible, because I was really looking forward to the party. Here's what I'm thinking. First, you could start the party without me, and I'll come as soon as I'm done. Second, if it takes too long, I could skip the dinner part and just join you for dessert. Or third, if I really can't make it, I'll take a rain check, and we can get together later this week. What do you think is best? Again, I'm so sorry. I'll make it up to you.

Yes, I have. A couple of years ago, I planned a camping trip with a friend and her kid. We'd been looking forward to it for weeks. I had packed the car the night before, and we were all set. But at six in the morning, my friend called me. Her little kid woke up with a high fever. He was burning up. We were really worried, so she rushed him to the emergency room. It turned out to be the flu. The doctor said he needed to rest. So, of course, we had to cancel the trip. The kid was so disappointed. I didn't want the day to be a total loss, so I came up with a plan B. When he felt a little better, I went over and set up the camping tent in their living room! We ate hot dogs and marshmallows on the floor, and we told stories with a flashlight. He laughed and said, "This is the best camping ever!" It wasn't the trip we'd planned, but it turned out great.

Yes, I've noticed a lot of changes. In Korea, most people live in apartments, and the new ones are very different from the old ones. First, new apartments have bigger living rooms and open kitchens. Ten years ago, kitchens were small and closed off. Second, they're a lot smarter. You can control the lights, heating, and even the elevator with your phone, or by talking to a wall panel. Third, there's better sound insulation, because noise from the floor above used to be a huge problem. Also, there's more storage, and some places have electric car chargers in the parking lot. My apartment is a bit older, so I don't have all of that. But every time I visit a friend's new place, I think, "Wow, I'm so jealous!"

Yes, I remember something like that here in my city. A few years ago, a company announced a plan to build a huge new apartment complex near my neighborhood. At first, it sounded great, because we needed more homes. But then people started to complain. Some worried about traffic. The roads were already busy in the morning, and thousands of new cars would make it a nightmare. Others were concerned about schools, because the local schools were already full. And some people said, "Why build so many? What if nobody moves in?" Because the local economy goes up and down, that was a real concern. There were meetings, and it was in the local news for weeks. In the end, they made the complex smaller, and they added a new road. I think that was a good compromise. As a resident, I was glad people spoke up.
